name: JBW theory (just be white)

lead: JBW, short for 'just be white', is a theory on looksmax.org and similar forums that white ethnicity gives a man an advantage in dating and in other areas of life, regardless of facial attractiveness.
Its relevance to looks is that it frames ethnicity as a factor that outweighs or modifies features. Community members dispute it in threads both supporting and challenging it [1][2][3].

paras: It is a framework for interpreting dating outcomes rather than a routine. Members cite anecdotes, dating-app experiments and social patterns, and others post counterexamples.
The theory is contested within forums and is discussed alongside broader debates. Researchers have studied racial preferences in online dating and report varied results by group and gender [4].

angle.text: JBW is an interpretive theory in which ethnicity is treated as a major determinant of dating outcomes. It is debated by forum users and has no direct intervention attached; members who accept it often discuss it when weighing how much appearance work can change their odds.

lead: JBW theory ('just be white') is a claim in looksmaxxing communities that being white gives a man a dating advantage that other traits struggle to match. It is usually phrased as a shorthand: where a poster believes the facial or physical gap between two men is small, ethnicity is said to decide the outcome. Some posters extend it beyond dating to jobs and social networks [1].

In looksmaxxing terms the theory is relevant because it sets the ceiling on what a person thinks appearance work can achieve. Believers describe white men as favoured in Western contexts and say non-white men face a handicap that grooming, fitness or surgery only partly offsets [1][2]. Other members argue the opposite, pointing to same-race pairings, Asian pop culture and their own experience [3][4], while some threads claim confirmation from dating-app tests [5]. The phrase is part of a family of '-pill' and 'theory' terms, such as the black pill, used to explain attraction in the community [6].

Academic work on racial patterns in online dating exists and is cited on Wikipedia. Studies report that white men receive more messages from Black, Asian and Hispanic women than from men of their own race, that Asian American men and Black women face particular disadvantages, and that findings differ by gender, group and platform. Researchers offer competing explanations, including socioeconomic status, exposure, media portrayals and bias. None of this research tests JBW as a theory.
infobox: Whiteness advantages dating (and sometimes career) outcomes

paras: The claim is summarised by posters in a few words: being white is a decisive advantage in the dating market, and being non-white is a handicap that is hard to offset. One thread titled 'Just Be White' quotes members saying it is 'over' most of the time for non-white men [2]. Thread titles such as 'just be white theory is legit' and 'just be white and have blue eyes bro' show the idea recurring in the forum across years, with some posters adding specific traits such as eye colour [7][8].

The term is used in two ways. In its strong form, ethnicity outweighs face, height and status. In weaker forms, posters say ethnicity is one factor among several, or that the 'white' advantage differs by region and by the woman's own background. One thread argues that the preference is 'for Asian women it is just be white, for Slavic Russian women just be German or Anglo', extending the idea into a ladder of ethnic preference [9]. Another discusses where Mediterranean men fit within the theory [10].

Wikipedia traces looksmaxxing's origins to now-defunct forums such as PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, where the PSL scale and much of the community's vocabulary developed [6]. Threads titled 'just be white' on looksmax.org appear among both older and newer threads [11][12], and the topic remained active in 2024 and 2025 [1][2][3][4].

Some members have said they apply the idea in practice. One thread claims that running 'just be white game' on YouTube was working for its author, and another proposes a channel travelling to non-white countries in order to test the theory on camera [13][14]. Other threads declare the theory 'over' after a counterexample or call themselves its 'king' [15][16]. These posts are individual claims, not systematic data.

Believers argue that whiteness matters beyond dating. A looksmax.org post argues the idea applies to everything in life, citing family connections, name-based resume screening and who holds executive roles in the West [1]. Others claim that dating-app experiments confirmed it, including a thread that also argues a competing 'just be Black' idea was disproved [5].

Another line of argument ties the advantage to social class rather than looks, claiming that women from lower-middle-class backgrounds especially prefer white men [17]. Posters who accept the theory frequently advise staying within one's own ethnic group or 'playing defensively', and some call white women the most sought-after group [2].

Opposing threads dispute the theory on the community's own terms. One argues that attractive East Asian women mostly partner with East Asian men in the United States, that the rise of K-pop raised the perceived appeal of East Asian men, and that white-man/Asian-woman pairings are not evidence of a universal preference [3]. Another thread, titled as a debunking of the theory, calls it a defeatist idea [4]. These posts are phrased with the community's usual harsh slang and are made by members describing their own observations and reading of marriage patterns, not published statistics.

Social scientists have studied racial patterns in online dating, and the findings differ by group, gender and platform. Wikipedia summarises several studies. Feliciano (2009) analysed profiles of white internet daters and reported that white women were more likely than white men to exclude Asian and Latino partners, while both groups excluded Black partners at high rates, and a later paper by Robnett and Feliciano (2011) largely replicated the gendered pattern. Hitsch, Hortaçsu and Ariely (2006) reported that race affects the response a user receives, with effects that vary by gender and race. Curington, Lundquist and Lin (2021) wrote that heterosexual white men are messaged more often by Black, Asian and Hispanic women than by men of their own race, while white women do not gain the same advantage, and they attribute part of this to the weight women place on socioeconomic status.

The same literature reports patterns that do not fit a single rule. Asian American men are reported as disadvantaged in several datasets even with higher education and income, East Asian women are frequently reported among the most responded-to women, and Black women among the least. Yancey (2009) found that Hispanic and Asian respondents were more willing to date white partners than Black partners. Researchers also disagree on interpretation: some scholars describe such patterns as sexual racism, while others describe them as personal preference, a debate noted by Callander, Newman and Holt (2015). Proposed explanations include socioeconomic status, media portrayals, exposure to other groups, regional and religious context, and evolutionary arguments.

Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing states that the subculture has been described, citing several sources, as also based on white supremacy, and quotes journalist Becca Rothfeld as saying its stalwarts regularly use racial slurs [6]. Within the forums, ethnicity-centred theories such as JBW are among the topics in which racial attitudes are most openly discussed; critics outside the community describe such discussion as racialised, while members describe it as an attempt to explain observed dating outcomes [6][1][3].

JBW functions mainly as a lens for self-assessment. Members who accept it use it to calibrate expectations, to argue about whether appearance or ethnicity is the more important variable, and to interpret dating-app results. Members who reject it use it as a foil in arguments about the strength of facial attractiveness, which most of the community's other frameworks, such as PSL ratings, treat as the main driver of success [6]. The theory has no associated product or procedure; it appears alongside, and sometimes in competition with, advice on skincare, fitness, hair and surgery.
No studies found. Studies of racial preferences in online dating, described above, are related research on a broader subject and do not test JBW as formulated.

lore.intro: JBW is a recurring topic on looksmax.org, with threads both defending and rebutting it, and with posters applying it to dating, jobs and social networks [1][2][3][4].

timeline.event: Phua and Kaufman publish an early study of how racial traits feature in online ads, an early study in the online-dating race literature summarised on Wikipedia.
Hitsch, Hortaçsu and Ariely report that race affects response rates on an online dating site, varying by gender and race.
Feliciano publishes 'Gendered racial exclusion among white internet daters' and Yancey reports racial preference patterns among Black, Hispanic and Asian Americans.
Robnett and Feliciano publish a follow-up in Social Forces that largely replicates the gendered exclusion pattern.
Callander, Newman and Holt study sexual racism among gay and bisexual white men, framing the preference-versus-racism debate.
Curington, Lundquist and Lin publish The Dating Divide, arguing online dating can amplify racial biases.
A looksmax.org thread argues JBW is disproven, citing East Asian pairings and pop culture.[3]
Threads such as 'Just Be White' and 'Just Be White Isn't a Joke' continue to circulate on looksmax.org.[1][2]
